work: The Genealogies of Our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ
author: Lord Arthur Hervey
ref: Hervey 1853, ch. II, note on p. 9 (quoting J. Mill, Vindication of our Lord's Genealogies, p. 182)
english: "...and that Petrus Galatinus, in the 16th century, was apparently the first of the Roman communion who did so. He mentions Spanheim, Luther, Chemnitz, Gomar, as having advocated this view." (Hervey's English; 'did so' = transferred both genealogies from the legal father to Mary, as reported from Mill)
page: p. 9 (note), printed page inferred from running head and PDF offset; confirmed by 'p. 57' and 'p. 95' cross-check
edition: Hervey, 1853, archive.org scan 'genealogiesofour00herv' (imprint on ad page: Macmillan & Co., Cambridge)
what_it_says: Mill reports (via Hervey) that no Father transferred the genealogies to Mary, and that Petrus Galatinus in the 16th century was apparently the first Roman Catholic to do so; Spanheim, Luther, Chemnitz and Gomar are named as advocates.
limits: Secondhand: Mill's Vindication (p. 182 as cited) was not opened. Hervey does not quote Galatinus's own words. 'First' is Mill's claim, not checked.
memory_only: Galatinus's book (De arcanis catholicae veritatis, c. 1518) and his date: from memory, UNVERIFIED.

work: The Genealogies of Our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ (note quoting J. Maldonatus, Commentary on Matthew 1)
author: Lord Arthur Hervey (quoting Juan Maldonado / Maldonatus)
date: pseudo-Jerome tract: unknown (medieval); Maldonatus c. 1590s (memory, UNVERIFIED)
ref: Hervey 1853, Notes, note on p. 354 (on Matthew 1 'Liber generationis'); Maldonatus, Commentarius in Matthaeum, ch. 1 (not opened)
original: Nec Augustino displicet. Mihi quoque placeret, nisi viderem evangelistas verum Josephi genus describere voluisse
original_edition: Latin as printed in Hervey 1853 (PDF text layer, scan pdf p. 384); these are Maldonatus's words as quoted by Hervey, not checked against Maldonatus's own edition.
english: Hervey's English note: Maldonatus, alluding to the opinion of the author of the tract 'De ortu Beatae Virginis', falsely ascribed to St Jerome (quoted as Jerome's by Annius of Viterbo), that Mary was the daughter of Eli, says 'Nec Augustino displicet' and adds 'Mihi quoque placeret, nisi viderem evangelistas verum Josephi genus describere voluisse'. (Hervey's own translation; no translator named)
page: p. 354 (note; pdf p. 384; offset 30 confirmed by printed 353 and 355 on neighbouring PDF pages)
what_it_says: Maldonatus reports that a tract ascribed to Jerome says Mary was the daughter of Eli (Luke's Heli), and says he himself would like this view were it not that the evangelists describe Joseph's lineage.
limits: The pseudo-Jerome tract was NOT opened: its text on Heli is unverified, and the search for it (WebSearch, Bodleian catalogue) found nothing on its genealogy. Hervey's 'Vhylnis' is an OCR/print error (probably 'Virginis'). Annius's claim is only described here.
memory_only: Date of the pseudo-Jerome tract and Maldonatus's commentary: not verified here.

work: The Genealogies of Our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ (note quoting Annius of Viterbo)
author: Lord Arthur Hervey (quoting Annius of Viterbo)
ref: Hervey 1853, ch. III (p. 95 note): Annius on the binomial/trinomial names of Judah's kings
original: "Ab isto Joas atque deinceps in reraemorationem reges semper binomii atque trinomii fuerunt. Nam iste primus dictus Elyh, Joas, Simeon. Item Her, Manasses; Ezechias, Jesus (i.e. Joses)."
original_edition: Latin as printed in Hervey 1853 (OCR; the scan reads 'reraemorationem'), quoting Annius's forged 'Philo'; Annius's own edition not checked
english: Hervey's English: "Even Annius of Viterbo in the 15th century thought this binomial theory required some extraneous support, and therefore forged an historical statement, as from Philo, that the kings of Judah from Joash downwards had all either two or three names."
what_it_says: Per Hervey, Annius invented a pseudo-Philonic statement to support double and triple names for Judah's kings, which Hervey treats as a forgery; this is evidence on Annius's reliability, not on the Lk=Mary reading.
limits: Hervey's claim about Annius's forgery is not checked against Annius's text or modern scholarship. The page does not mention Mary or Heli.
memory_only: Annius of Viterbo, Commentaria (Rome, 1498) and the Lk=Mary reading attributed to him: from memory, UNVERIFIED; Hervey's note also says Annius quoted the Eli tract as Jerome's (see item 2).

work: The Genealogies of Our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ
author: Lord Arthur Hervey
ref: Hervey 1853, ch. III, sect. III, p. 57
english: "...not only are both the genealogies Joseph's, but that both are also Mary's. For if the Matthan of St Matthew is the same individual as the Matthat of St Luke, it follows that Jacob and Heli were own brothers. And if Mary were the daughter of Jacob, and Joseph the son of Heli, Joseph and Mary would be first cousins..."
page: p. 57 (pdf p. 87; running head 'Section III, These genealogies are framed')
what_it_says: Hervey's own view: both lists are Joseph's and also Mary's, with Matthan=Matthat, Jacob and Heli as brothers, Mary the daughter of Jacob and Joseph the son of Heli.
limits: Hervey's own proposal (a levirate-style reconstruction); it is not a witness to any earlier writer.

work: The Genealogies of Our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ
author: Lord Arthur Hervey
ref: Hervey 1853, ch. III, p. 130 (text on Matthan, Jacob and Heli)
english: "Jacob I suppose to have had no son, but to have been the father of the Virgin Mary: Heli, the father of Joseph. Joseph, according to universal Jewish custom, took Mary his cousin to wife, and was thus on every account Jacob's successor and heir."
page: p. 130 (pdf p. 160; running head 'Harmony of the Genealogies 130')
what_it_says: Hervey makes Jacob (of Matthew) the father of Mary and Heli (of Luke) the father of Joseph, with Joseph and Mary first cousins by a Jewish marriage custom.
limits: Hervey's own reconstruction; cites Jewish custom without a source here. 'Universal Jewish custom' is an assertion, not checked.

work: The Genealogies of Our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ
author: Lord Arthur Hervey
ref: Hervey 1853, ch. III, p. 48 (on Julius Africanus's scheme and the levirate solution)
english: "...the scheme proposed by Africanus, and apparently adopted by Eusebius and other fathers after him, is neither on the ground of authority, nor of any obstacle in the way of a more intrinsic merit, probable explanation of the difficulty before us. Neither is there any truth in the notion first broached by Africanus, and since repeated by many others, that the term 'begat' used by St..." (sentence continues; OCR-cut)
what_it_says: Hervey treats Africanus's levirate scheme as the (older) explanation, adopted by Eusebius, and criticises another claim said to be first broached by Africanus.
limits: The continuation of the sentence about 'begat' is cut in the OCR; full text needs a clean scan. Hervey is himself a critic of the Africanus scheme.

work: Horae Hebraicae et Talmudicae (Exercitations upon St Matthew, vol. II)
author: John Lightfoot
ref: Lightfoot, Exercitations upon St Matthew, ch. 1 ver. 16 (Mt 1:16), p. 14
original_edition: Latin original not checked; the scan is the English Pitman 1859 reprint
english: "Hence the reason may very easily be given, why Matthew brings down the generation to Joseph, Mary's husband; but Luke to Eli, Mary's father. These two frame the genealogy two ways, according to the double notion of the promise of Christ."
translator: not named in the scan (the Pitman editor notes that the translator was not known; the translation is said to be the one published by Strype)
page: p. 14 (pdf p. 20; running head 'Horae Hebraicae and Talmudical ... 14')
what_it_says: Lightfoot holds that Matthew traces Joseph (Mary's husband) while Luke traces Eli, Mary's father, the two lists framing the royal and the human side of the promise.
limits: This is an early-modern reading (Lightfoot) and is not the earliest Lk=Mary text; Lightfoot gives no evidence in this passage, only the 'mother's family' argument.
memory_only: Lightfoot's Latin dates: from memory, UNVERIFIED.

work: Horae Hebraicae et Talmudicae (Chorographical century, vol. I)
author: John Lightfoot
ref: Lightfoot, Chorographical century, 'Jabneh/Jamnia' section, p. 94: Talmudic story of Simeon ben Shetach and the eighty witches (Lightfoot cites Hieros. Sanhedr. fol. 23.3; Bab. Sanhedr. fol. 44.2 'in Glossa')
original_edition: Hebrew Talmud not located in the scan's own Hebrew; checked in Sefaria only (see limits)
english: "...He saw Mary, the daughter of Eli, in the shades, hung up by the kernels of the breasts; and when he inquired, How long she was to suffer those things? it was answered, Until Simon Ben Shetach came to supply her place." Lightfoot adds: "Let the learned reader turn this clause into English; unless my conjecture fail me, it savours of spite and poison. I should thus render it:"
translator: not named in the scan (Pitman 1859 English; translator not identified)
page: p. 94 (pdf p. 44; running head '94 Chorographical century')
what_it_says: Lightfoot renders a Talmudic-style story with a 'Mary the daughter of Eli' tormented in the shades. Strauss (p. 101 note) cites this same passage as the Jewish source that 'took the genealogy of Luke ... for that of Mary'.
limits: The name 'Mary daughter of Eli' is Lightfoot's own rendering with an admitted conjecture ('unless my conjecture fail me'). Sefaria Hebrew of Jerusalem Talmud Sanhedrin 6:9 (5 segments, no such story or name) and Bavli Sanhedrin 44b-45b (the Shimon ben Shetach 'eighty women in Ashkelon' line, no name) were checked and show no 'Miriam/Mary daughter of Eli'. The Venice-edition Yerushalmi fol. 23c and the 'Glossa' were not checked. So the Talmud claim is UNVERIFIED and currently NOT found.
memory_only: The Venice-edition folio numbers and the 'Glossa' reading: from memory, not checked.

work: A Harmony of the Gospels for Students of the Life of Christ
author: A. T. Robertson
ref: Robertson 1922, Notes on Special Points, sect. 5 'The Two Genealogies of Christ', p. 259 (opening paragraph)
english: "Sceptics of all ages, from Porphyry and Celsus to Strauss, have urged the impossibility of reconciling the difficulties in the two accounts of the descent of Jesus. Even Alford says it is impossible to reconcile them."
edition: Robertson, 1922, archive.org scan 'harmonyofgospels00robeuoft' (Harper, per record; not checked)
what_it_says: Robertson states the classic objection (Porphyry, Celsus, Strauss, Alford) that the two genealogies cannot be reconciled, and then lists the solutions that follow.
limits: Robertson's account of who said what is secondhand. The list of objectors is not exhaustive.

work: A Harmony of the Gospels for Students of the Life of Christ
author: A. T. Robertson
ref: Robertson 1922, Notes on Special Points, sect. 5(1b), p. 259
english: "These omissions are after Joram, the names of Ahaziah, Joash, Amaziah, and after Josiah, these of Jehoiakim and Eliakim ... But such omissions were very common in the Old Testament genealogies. See 2 Chron. 22:9." (OCR reads 'Aliaziah')
what_it_says: Robertson explains Matthew's omissions (Ahaziah, Joash, Amaziah; Jehoiakim, Eliakim) as usual in OT lists; 'son' can mean descendant, and the omitted kings do not invalidate the line.
limits: Robertson says the omissions are 'common in the OT'; his 14x3 explanation (David counted in two sets) is in the same section but not quoted here.

work: A Harmony of the Gospels for Students of the Life of Christ
author: A. T. Robertson
ref: Robertson 1922, Notes on Special Points, sect. 5(2a), p. 260
english: "(a) As early as Julius Africanus it was suggested that the two lines had united in accordance with the law of Levirate marriage. By this theory, Heli and Jacob being stepbrothers, Jacob married Heli's widow and was the real father of Joseph. Thus both genealogies would be the descent of Joseph, one the real, the other the legal."
what_it_says: Robertson gives Africanus's levirate theory as the first explanation (both lists Joseph's, one natural and one legal), and names McClellan and Waddy as its advocates.
limits: Robertson's summary; Africanus's own words are in item 20 (Eusebius HE 1.7.17).

work: A Harmony of the Gospels for Students of the Life of Christ
author: A. T. Robertson
ref: Robertson 1922, Notes on Special Points, sect. 5(2c), pp. 260-261
english: "(c) The third and most plausible solution yet suggested makes Matthew give the real descent of Joseph, and Luke the real descent of Mary. ... So practically Luther, Bengel, Olshausen, Lightfoot, Wieseler, Robinson, Alexander, Godet, Weiss, Andrews ... and many recent writers." (OCR 'Wdss' read as Weiss). Plummer: "thinks it incredible that Mary's genealogy should be given by Luke."
what_it_says: Robertson reports that the Lk=Mary solution was held by Luther, Bengel, Lightfoot and others, while Plummer found it incredible; Robertson himself calls it the most plausible.
limits: Robertson's list is secondhand and mixes Protestant and modern writers; no date of origin is given for the Lk=Mary reading. Bacon (1911) is reported to say most scholars abandon reconciliation.

work: Commentary on the Gospel of Luke, vol. I
author: Frédéric Louis Godet
ref: Godet, Commentary on Luke 3:23-38, p. 199 (sect. on 'the genealogical document')
english: "...2d. That the genealogical document which he consulted began with the name of Heli; 3d. And consequently, that this piece was not originally the genealogy of Jesus or of Joseph, but of Heli." (OCR 'od.' read as '3d.')
translator: E. W. Shalders, B.A. (from the second French edition; T. & T. Clark, Edinburgh, 1875)
page: p. 199 (pdf p. 215; running head '199 CHAP. III. 23-33')
edition: Godet, T. & T. Clark, 1875, archive.org 'commentaryongo01gode', vol. I
what_it_says: Godet argues that Luke's list was from a document beginning with Heli, so Luke's list was not originally Joseph's, and he treats Jesus as Heli's descendant through Mary (his conclusion is developed later).
limits: Godet's 'Heli' document reading is not identical to the Mary's-father reading; Robertson reports Godet as favouring Lk=Mary. Full conclusion not checked.

work: The Life of Jesus, Critically Examined (Eng. tr. of 4th German ed.)
author: David Friedrich Strauss
date: German 1835-36; English 1846 (translator Marian Evans / George Eliot); this scan NY 1860
ref: Strauss, section 20 ('The two genealogies of Jesus considered separately' per contents), p. 101 (text and footnote)
english: "The opinion that Mary was of the race of David as well as Joseph has been long held. ... many apocryphal writers clearly state this opinion, as well as Justin Martyr, whose expression, that the virgin was of the race of David, Jacob, Isaac, and Abraham, may be considered an indication that he applied to Mary one of our genealogies..." Footnote: "The Jews also in their representation of a Mary, the daughter of Heli, tormented in the lower world, (see Lightfoot,) appear to have taken the genealogy of Luke, which sets out from Heli, for that of Mary."
translator: Marian Evans (George Eliot), 1846 translation; this copy NY: Calvin Blanchard, 1860, vol. I
page: p. 101 (pdf p. 117; running head 'Genealogical tables of Matthew and Luke 101'); footnote on p. 101 (OCR '1 Lightfoot horae p. 7?0' unclear)
what_it_says: Strauss says the Davidic descent of Mary was long held, that apocryphal writers and Justin support it, and that the Jewish 'Mary daughter of Heli' tradition (citing Lightfoot) is an example of the Heli-Mary reading.
limits: The footnote's Lightfoot page reference is unclear in the OCR. Strauss's footnote list of defenders (Spanheim, Lightfoot, Michaelis, Paulus, Kuinoel, Olshausen, Hoffmann) is attached in the OCR without clear anchoring.

work: The Life of Jesus, Critically Examined
author: David Friedrich Strauss
ref: Strauss, section 22 'The genealogies unhistorical' (opening paragraph), p. 102; the 'impossible to apply' sentence closes the preceding section on the same page
english: "...which unavoidably embarrass every attempt to bring these two genealogies into harmony with one another, will lead us to despair of reconciling them, and will incline us to acknowledge, with the more free-thinking class of critics, that they are mutually contradictory." ... "...it is impossible to apply the genealogy of the third Evangelist to Mary."
translator: Marian Evans (George Eliot), 1846; this copy NY 1860
page: p. 102 (pdf p. 118; running head '102 THE LIFE OF JESUS')
what_it_says: Strauss holds that the two genealogies are irreconcilable and cannot apply to Mary; he uses this to reject the Lk=Mary reading.
limits: Strauss's own argument on Luke 1:27 and 2:4 ('the genealogy of the third Evangelist cannot be applied to Mary') is not answered here.

work: The Virgin Birth of Christ
author: J. Gresham Machen
ref: Machen 1930, ch. 'The Integrity of the Lucan Narrative', p. 127 (on Lk 1:27 and Mary's descent)
english: "Certainly her kinship with Elisabeth does not preclude such an opinion; for intermarriage between the tribe of Levi, to which Elisabeth belonged, and the other tribes was perfectly permissible under the law. No positive objection, therefore, can be raised to the view, which is held even by some scholars who reject the reference of the words 'of the house of David' in Lk. i.27 to Mary, that the narrator means to imply ... that Mary as well as Joseph was descended from David."
page: p. 127 (pdf p. 145; the page sits between the running heads of p. 126 (pdf 144) and p. 128 (pdf 146))
what_it_says: Machen answers the Levite objection: Elisabeth's Levitical kinship (Lk 1:36) does not rule out Mary's Davidic descent, because Levi-Judah intermarriage was lawful.
limits: Machen argues from the Mosaic permission only; it is not a historical argument about Mary's actual family. Machen himself says the Davidic descent of Mary is not stated in the narrative.

work: The Virgin Birth of Christ
author: J. Gresham Machen
ref: Machen 1930, note 19 on p. 128, citing W. Bauer, Das Leben Jesu im Zeitalter der neutestamentlichen Apokryphen (1909), pp. 8-16, esp. p. 11
english: "Passages in the early patristic period declaring Jesus to belong to Levi as well as to Judah, Bauer says, do not mean that while Joseph was descended from Judah, Mary was descended from Levi; ... 'In the time before Origen,' says Bauer, 'Mary is nowhere clearly designated as a daughter of Levi' (p. 11). On the other hand, the Davidic descent of Mary appears, Bauer points out, in the Protevangelium of James and other apocryphal Gospels, in Justin Martyr, Tertullian, etc., and in the Sinaitic Syriac manuscript..."
what_it_says: Per Bauer (as quoted by Machen), no writer before Origen calls Mary a daughter of Levi, while several early writers give her Davidic descent.
limits: Bauer's book was not opened; the quote is Machen's rendering. Machen's p. 11 reference is to Bauer, not to a primary text. The Old Syriac and Tertullian claims are not checked.
memory_only: Bauer 1909 text and page numbers: from Machen only.

work: The Virgin Birth of Christ
author: J. Gresham Machen
ref: Machen 1930, p. 129 (on 'begat' in Mt 1), citing F. C. Burkitt, Evangelion da-Mepharreshe (1904), vol. I, pp. 260 ff. (note 21)
english: "...F. C. Burkitt ... maintains that the word 'begat' in the Matthaean genealogy does not indicate physical paternity, but only the transmission of legal heirship, so that even if the genealogy had ended with the words, 'Joseph begat Jesus,' that would not have afforded the slightest indication that the author did not believe in the virgin birth."
what_it_says: Burkitt (as quoted by Machen) reads Matthew's 'begat' as legal heirship, so the Matthean line does not by itself show physical paternity.
limits: Burkitt's text not opened; quoted by Machen. Note 21 cites Burkitt p. 260 ff. Some scholars reject this reading of 'begat' (Hervey, item 6).

work: The Life and Times of Jesus the Messiah, vol. I
author: Alfred Edersheim
ref: Edersheim, book II ch. 'The Betrothal of Joseph and Mary', pp. 148-149
english: "Whatever view may be taken of the genealogies in the Gospels according to St. Matthew and St. Luke—whether they be regarded as those of Joseph and of Mary, or, which seems the more likely, as those of Joseph only, marking his natural and his legal descent from David..."
page: pp. 148-149 (the sentence runs from p. 148 to p. 149; 'THE BETROTHAL OF JOSEPH AND MARY' running head, p. 149)
edition: Edersheim, 1915 ed., archive.org 'lifetimesofjesus0001alfr_w3s0' (OCR text only; PDF not downloaded: >60 MB for the 1899 copy)
what_it_says: Edersheim says the genealogies may be read as Mary's or as Joseph's, but that it 'seems the more likely' they are Joseph's only, marking his natural and legal descent from David; he does not say here which list is which.
limits: Edersheim's appendix on the genealogies was not located in the vol. I scan; only this passage was read. 1883 first edition not checked.

work: Ecclesiastical History, Book I, ch. 7
author: Eusebius of Caesarea
date: c. 311-325 AD (Africanus's letter to Aristides c. 230 AD)
ref: Eusebius, HE 1.7.10 and 1.7.16-17 (quoting Julius Africanus, letter to Aristides)
original_edition: Greek not fetched (no open Greek edition read in this session; GCS Schwartz not opened)
english: "17. Thus far Africanus. And the lineage of Joseph being thus traced, Mary also is virtually shown to be of the same tribe with him, since, according to the law of Moses, intermarriages between different tribes were not permitted. For the command is to marry one of the same family and lineage, so that the inheritance may not pass from tribe to tribe."
translator: Arthur Cushman McGiffert (NPNF2 vol. 1, ed. Schaff & Wace)
page: book I, ch. 7, sect. 17 (NPNF2 page not checked)
what_it_says: Africanus (as quoted by Eusebius) says Joseph was by nature the son of Jacob but by law the son of Eli, and that Mary is of the same tribe as Joseph because tribal intermarriage was forbidden.
limits: English only. Africanus does not say Luke gives Mary's line; his solution is levirate with Joseph as the legal son of Eli. Mary's tribe is Judah by inference, not by any explicit Mary-genealogy.

work: The Harmony of the Gospels (De consensu evangelistarum), Book II, ch. 3
author: Augustine of Hippo
ref: Augustine, De consensu evangelistarum II.3.5 (on Matthew's 'begat' and Luke's 'adoption' of Joseph)
english: "...they might easily perceive that Joseph may have had two fathers — namely, one by whom he was begotten, and a second by whom he may have been adopted. For it was an ancient custom also among that people to adopt children..."
translator: S. D. F. Salmond (NPNF1 vol. 6, ed. Schaff)
page: Book II, ch. 3, sect. 5 (NPNF1 page not checked)
what_it_says: Augustine's solution: Luke gives Joseph's adoptive father's line and Matthew his natural (begetting) line, so Joseph had two fathers.
limits: This is an adoption solution, not a Lk=Mary solution. Augustine's Retractations (2.16) were not checked. The Maldonatus phrase 'Nec Augustino displicet' (item 2) is not checked against Augustine's text.
memory_only: Retractations 2.16 content: from memory, not checked.

work: Dialogue with Trypho, ch. 100
author: Justin Martyr
ref: Justin, Dialogue with Trypho 100 (Son of man; the Virgin 'of the family of David')
english: "...He said then that He was the Son of man, either because of His birth by the Virgin, who was, as I said, of the family of David and Jacob, and Isaac, and Abraham; or because Adam was the father both of Himself and of those who have been first enumerated from whom Mary derives her descent."
translator: Marcus Dods and George Reith (ANF vol. 1)
what_it_says: Justin says the Virgin Mary was of the family of David, Jacob, Isaac and Abraham, which Strauss (item 14) reads as Mary descending from David.
limits: English only; 'the family of David' is Justin's phrase in a christological argument. Justin does not say that Luke's list is Mary's.

work: Jeremiah 22:30 (Jeconiah / Coniah)
author: Jeremiah (prophet), Hebrew Bible
ref: Jeremiah 22:30
original: כֹּ֣ה ׀ אָמַ֣ר יְהֹוָ֗ה כִּתְב֞וּ אֶת־הָאִ֤ישׁ הַזֶּה֙ עֲרִירִ֔י גֶּ֖בֶר לֹא־יִצְלַ֣ח בְּיָמָ֑יו כִּי֩ לֹ֨א יִצְלַ֜ח מִזַּרְע֗וֹ אִ֚ישׁ יֹשֵׁב֙ עַל־כִּסֵּ֣א דָוִ֔ד וּמֹשֵׁ֥ל ע֖וֹד בִּיהוּדָֽה׃ {פ}
original_edition: Sefaria text 'Miqra according to the Masorah' (Hebrew with cantillation, BHS-style); not checked against the Leningrad codex image
english: "Thus saith the LORD: Write ye this man childless, A man that shall not prosper in his days; For no man of his seed shall prosper, Sitting upon the throne of David, And ruling any more in Judah."
translator: JPS 1917 (The Holy Scriptures: A New Translation, Public Domain), as displayed on Sefaria
edition: Sefaria: https://www.sefaria.org/api/texts/Jeremiah.22.30 (Hebrew 'Miqra according to the Masorah'; English JPS 1917)
what_it_says: Jeremiah says that no man of Coniah's (Jeconiah's) seed shall sit on David's throne, which is the basis of the Jeconiah-curse objection.
limits: The verse does not mention a genealogy or Mary; the objection depends on reading 'no seed' as a legal bar to a son (Matt/Luke) of Jeconiah. Compare Jer 36:30 (Jehoiakim) and 1 Chr 3:17 (see Lightfoot vol II, 1 Chr 3:17 comment). Not checked further.

work: Gospel of Luke 3:23
author: Luke (evangelist)
ref: Luke 3:23
original: Καὶ αὐτὸς ἦν Ἰησοῦς ἀρχόμενος ὡσεὶ ἐτῶν τριάκοντα ὢν υἱός ὡς ἐνομίζετο Ἰωσὴφ τοῦ Ἠλὶ
original_edition: Greek as printed in the biblehub.com interlinear (edition not named on the page; not checked against Nestle-Aland 28 or Westcott-Hort)
english: "And Jesus himself began to be about thirty years of age, being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph, which was the son of Heli," (KJV, as printed on biblehub interlinear)
translator: King James Version (as printed on biblehub)
what_it_says: Luke says Jesus was, as was supposed, the son of Joseph, son of Heli; the Greek ends 'ὡς ἐνομίζετο Ἰωσὴφ τοῦ Ἠλὶ' (with ἐνομίζετο 'was supposed').
limits: The Greek text is from a secondary display page; the source edition is not stated, so it counts as PARTLY. The meaning of 'son' in 3:23 is the disputed point (son of Joseph / son-in-law / grandson).

work: Gospel of Luke 1:5
author: Luke (evangelist)
ref: Luke 1:5
original: Ἐγένετο ἐν ταῖς ἡμέραις Ἡρῴδου βασιλέως τῆς Ἰουδαίας ἱερεύς τις ὀνόματι Ζαχαρίας ἐξ ἐφημερίας Ἀβιά καὶ γυνὴ αὐτῷ ἐκ τῶν θυγατέρων Ἀαρών καὶ τὸ ὄνομα αὐτῆς Ἐλισάβετ
original_edition: Greek as printed in the biblehub.com interlinear (edition not named; not checked)
english: "There was in the days of Herod, the king of Judaea, a certain priest named Zacharias, of the course of Abia: and his wife was of the daughters of Aaron, and her name was Elisabeth." (KJV, biblehub)
translator: King James Version (as printed on biblehub)
what_it_says: Elisabeth, wife of the priest Zacharias, was of the daughters of Aaron (so of Levi by descent).
limits: Establishes Elisabeth's priestly/Levitical kinship. It does not say Mary was from Levi.

work: Gospel of Luke 1:36
author: Luke (evangelist)
ref: Luke 1:36
original: καὶ ἰδοὺ Ἐλισάβετ ἡ συγγενίς σου καὶ αὐτὴ συνείληφεν υἱὸν ἐν γήρει αὐτῆς καὶ οὗτος μὴν ἕκτος ἐστὶν αὐτῇ τῇ καλουμένῃ στείρᾳ
original_edition: Greek as printed in the biblehub.com interlinear (edition not named; not checked)
english: "And, behold, thy cousin Elisabeth, she hath also conceived a son in her old age: and this is the sixth month with her, who was called barren." (KJV, biblehub; the Greek word is συγγενίς 'kinswoman')
translator: King James Version (as printed on biblehub)
what_it_says: Gabriel calls Elisabeth Mary's kinswoman (συγγενίς), which is the basis of the Levite-Mary argument.
limits: 'Kinswoman' does not say which tribe Mary belonged to; the Levite argument is an inference. Machen (item 16) answers that Levi-Judah intermarriage was lawful.

work: Gospel of Matthew 1:16
author: Matthew (evangelist)
ref: Matthew 1:16
original: Ἰακὼβ δὲ ἐγέννησεν τὸν Ἰωσὴφ τὸν ἄνδρα Μαρίας ἐξ ἧς ἐγεννήθη Ἰησοῦς ὁ λεγόμενος Χριστός
original_edition: Greek as printed in the biblehub.com interlinear (edition not named; not checked)
english: "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ." (KJV, biblehub)
translator: King James Version (as printed on biblehub)
what_it_says: Matthew ends the list with Jacob begetting Joseph, 'the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus', which is the 'Jacob father of Joseph' basis for the Mary-as-Jacob's-daughter reading (Hervey item 5).
limits: The Greek is from a secondary display page with no named edition (PARTLY). The phrase 'ἐξ ἧς' (of whom) is the textual point used by Mary-line readers.
